children: AstraZeneca expects an experimental treatment for a rare bone-and-muscle disorder to win regulatory approval, the head of its Alexion rare-disease unit said, despite the drug missing the main goal of a clinical trial.

Results from a late-stage clinical trial of the drug, efzimfotase alfa, showed efficacy in improving mobility, pain and fatigue in adolescents and adults with rare disease hypophosphatasia, Alexion Chief Executive Marc Dunoyer said in an interview.

"I'm very confident in the data that we have collected," Dunoyer said. "I believe that the totality of our evidence and the breadth of our evidence in different age groups will lead us to an approval."

AstraZeneca tested efzimfotase across three studies in different groups of patients with hypophosphatasia, a metabolic disease that can impair bone development and cause muscle weakness, fatigue and pain. Two studies in children up to 12 years of age met their primary objectives, but a third with adolescents and adults fell short of the target.

The company on Sunday presented the full data of the study that missed the goal at the annual meeting of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research in Boston, and said the lack of a statistically significant improvement in mobility was largely due to better-than-expected results in the placebo group.
"We believe we have confirmed efficacy in the totality of our evidence," Dunoyer said.
AstraZeneca developed efzimfotase alfa as a successor to its existing hypophosphatasia medicine Strensiq, which is approved for certain patients and generated $1.7 billion in revenue last year.
Dunoyer said the company is sticking to its forecast that efzimfotase alfa can generate annual sales of between $3 billion and $5 billion at its peak.
"If we get not as wide a label as we think and hope, it will be $3 billion. If we get as wide a label as we hope, it will be $5 billion," he said.

Efzimfotase alfa has potential to benefit a larger population of patients and reach more regions than its predecessor, as it is an easier product to adopt for doctors and patients due to its less frequent administration, Dunoyer said.
